title: Client-side flush coordination vs proxy buffering: experiment notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures a set of microbenchmarks and field-probe experiments that compare two broad approaches for minimizing end-to-end token latency in streaming inference: 1) client-side flush coordination (clients aggressively flush small chunks as soon as tokens are produced), and 2) proxy-side buffering (edge proxies coalesce small writes into larger frames before forwarding). We measured effects on p50/p95/p99 latency, tokenization throughput, and tail amplification under realistic bursty arrival patterns and with KV-cache warm/cold across HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2, and gRPC streams.

Motivation / problem statement:

- We observe two common sources of extra latency in production: small-client flush patterns (many small writes) and proxy buffering that adds micro- and macro-batching. Both can reduce endpoint load/cost but trade off tail latency.
- Hypothesis: Client flush coordination (intentional coalescing at the client) can reduce proxy amplification and give predictable latency, but requires client changes. Proxy buffering can be deployed centrally but may worsen tails under bursty traffic and interact poorly with KV-cache warmup.

Test matrix and knobs explored:

- Transports: HTTP/1.1 (chunked), HTTP/2, gRPC (HTTP/2-based streaming).
- Client modes: immediate-flush (every token), micro-batch (coalesce up to N ms or M bytes), adaptive (flush on punctuation or EOS).
- Proxy modes: pass-through (no buffering), small-coalesce (buffer up to 512B or 5ms), large-coalesce (buffer up to 8KB or 50ms), backpressure-aware (drop to pass-through when active connections > threshold).
- TCP-level knobs: Nagle on/off, TCP_CORK toggles in Linux kernel where applicable (edge proxy container), SO_SNDBUF sizes.
- Workloads: short-response (80 tokens median), long-response (1024 tokens median), bursty arrivals (Poisson + microbursts 200 req/sec for 500ms every 10s), KV cache states (cold, warm).

Bench machines and topology:

- Client harness: 4x m6i.large runners (custom harness using wrk2 + python driver), with synthetic token generator emitting token-per-ms profiles derived from real inference traces.
- Edge proxy: 2x c6i.xlarge running our edge-proxy image (current main branch + experimental buffering flags).
- Serving nodes: 6x GPU hosts running inference runtime (quantized models), pinned to us-west-2.
- All nodes in same VPC; we also ran an inter-region experiment (client in us-east-1, edge proxy us-west-2) to observe RTT magnification.

Measurement methodology:

- For streaming latency we measure: time from first client write to first byte of response (first-token latency), and time from request start to final token (completion). For streaming, we capture per-token timestamps where possible via a simple tracing header (x-trace-token-ts).
- Each experiment ran for 20 minutes steady-state after a 2-minute warmup. We recorded p50/p90/p95/p99 for first-token and completion, CPU/mem on proxy, TCP retransmits, and application-level reorders (rare).
- We repeated each configuration 3x and report average percentiles; variance shown in notes below.

Key observations (short):

1) Immediate client flush + proxy pass-through: best median first-token latency for short responses (p50 improved by 10–15% vs other combos), but p99 is worse under bursts (tail amplification) because many small writes cause proxy queuing and kernel scheduler overhead.

2) Client micro-batching (5ms or 512B) + proxy pass-through: most consistent tail behavior and near-median latency of immediate flush. This was a robust middle-ground for HTTP/2 and gRPC.

3) Proxy small-coalesce (5ms/512B) with immediate client flush: reduced number of egress writes by ~60%, lower proxy CPU by ~20%, but increased p99 by 8–25ms depending on workload. For long responses this overhead amortized and was negligible.

4) Large proxy coalescing (50ms/8KB) increased cold-KV warmup completion time by up to 35% because proxy buffering delayed early tokens, which delayed KV cache population heuristics in the runtime (we're using heuristic-driven KV store warm paths tied to first-token arrival).

5) TCP Nagle disabled at client improved performance only when proxy was pass-through. When proxy buffered aggressively, Nagle was less relevant. Using TCP_CORK to control kernel level coalescing on proxy gave similar results to application-level buffering but is less flexible for policy-based backpressure.

6) HTTP/2 internal frame coalescing: because HTTP/2 has explicit flow-control windows, proxy buffering interacts with stream window sizes. In experiments where client flushes produced many small frames, p99 increased due to WINDOW_UPDATE timing. Raising initial stream window on proxy mitigated this but increased memory usage under heavy concurrency.

Representative numbers (short-response, bursty arrival):

- Config A (client immediate, proxy pass-through): first-token p50=18ms, p95=62ms, p99=148ms; completion p50=110ms, p95=320ms, p99=640ms.
- Config B (client micro-batch 5ms/512B, proxy pass-through): first-token p50=19ms, p95=45ms, p99=92ms; completion p50=130ms, p95=210ms, p99=380ms.
- Config C (client immediate, proxy small-coalesce 5ms/512B): first-token p50=28ms, p95=76ms, p99=210ms; completion p50=120ms, p95=260ms, p99=510ms.

(Notes: numbers are averages across 3 runs; variance up to ±8% on p95/p99 between runs.)

Interesting emergent behavior and micro-details:

- Tail amplification often correlated with proxy CPU spikes due to epoll wakeups caused by many small writes; reducing write syscall rate (client micro-batching) removed that correlation.
- In gRPC streams, the server runtime sometimes delayed emitting the first token by a few ms when it observed delayed WINDOW_UPDATE frames; this suggested the runtime's own gRPC stub/transport library is sensitive to pacing and windowing semantics.
- When proxy buffered but also applied backpressure heuristics (e.g., bypass buffering when active connections > 120), we saw best-of-both-worlds: lower average CPU and bounded tails. Implemented as a simple LRU tracking + active connection count in edge-proxy.

Operational implications / recommendations:

- Short-term (deployable): enable client micro-batching guidelines in SDKs by default (5ms / 512B heuristics) for streaming endpoints. Add example wrappers in python/node SDKs. This yields consistent tails without central infra changes.
- Medium-term: implement adaptive proxy buffering with a backpressure-aware bypass path (already prototyped in PR 432). Policy: coalesce up to X ms or Y bytes but bypass when active connections exceed threshold or observed per-connection syscall rate crosses threshold.
- Long-term: invest in transport-level observability (per-stream write syscall counts, kernel wakeups) surfaced in Console to detect write-amplification patterns per customer. Also evaluate whether runtime can emit an explicit 'first-token-ready' signal to eliminate heuristics that depend on first-token arrival for KV cache warm paths.

Open questions / TODOs:

- We need to test with real customer traffic (with PII scrubbed) to confirm burstiness characteristics differ from synthetic bursts. Ticket: JIRA INF-2489 (data request).
- How will proxy buffering interact with TLS record coalescing at our frontmost TLS terminators (we tested non-TLS and TLS-on-proxy but not TLS-terminator + internal proxy buffering). Action: replicate experiment with TLS termination at LB + plain proxy behind LB.
- Explore lowering initial HTTP/2 stream window vs increasing it: cost/benefit for memory vs lower WINDOW_UPDATE sensitivity.

Mini-playbook for reproducing locally:

1) Build edge-proxy with experimental flags: make build && docker build -t edge-proxy:buf-exp .
2) Run simple harness: ./bench/run_stream_harness.py --clients 200 --rate 50 --pattern bursty --client-mode immediate --proxy-mode pass-through --duration 20m --trace-header x-trace-token-ts
3) Collect traces: curl localhost:9411/trace?service=edge-proxy and export to CSV for pXX calculation.

Conclusions:

- Client libraries should default to a small micro-batching policy for streaming (5ms/512B) to avoid the majority of tail cases without central infra rollouts.
- Proxy buffering is a useful lever to reduce egress syscall and CPU at the edge, but it must be adaptive and backpressure-aware to avoid tail amplification and negative interactions with KV-cache warmup and HTTP/2 flow control.
- We can get better operational visibility by surfacing per-connection syscall/write-rate metrics and by instrumenting the runtime to decouple KV-cache warm heuristics from first-token arrival where possible.

Appendix: quick checklist for SDK change (Priya/Zoe):

- [ ] Add micro-batch wrapper in python SDK (default: 5ms or 512B) with opt-out.
- [ ] Add example in node SDK + doc blurb in streaming README.
- [ ] Add telemetry header to trace write counts (x-client-write-count) and stitch in Console.
- [ ] Coordinate rollout with edge-proxy PR 432 (Luca) to enable adaptive buffering flags behind a runtime feature flag.

End of notes.
